{{Short description|Problem requiring a choice between equally undesirable alternatives}}
{{Other uses}}
[[File:A Dilemma (BM 1945,0109.26).jpg|thumb|Cartoon showing [[William Ewart Gladstone]] in a dilemma: If he climbs to escape the guard dog he will face the man's wrath, but if he drops to avoid the man, the dog will attack him.]]

A '''dilemma''' ({{etymology|grc|''{{Wikt-lang|grc|δίλημμα}}'' ({{grc-transl|δίλημμα}})|double [[lemma (logic)|proposition]]}}) is a [[problem solving|problem]] offering two possibilities, neither of which is unambiguously acceptable or preferable. The possibilities are termed the ''horns'' of the dilemma, a [[cliché]]d usage, but distinguishing the dilemma from other kinds of predicament as a matter of usage.<ref>{{cite book |last=Garner|first=Bryan |author-link=Bryan A. Garner |title=[[Garner's Modern English Usage|Garner's Modern American Usage]] |date=2009 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=9780199888771 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=FwmQpyibKkAC&pg=PA257 257] |language=en}}</ref>

==Terminology==
The term ''dilemma'' is attributed by [[Gabriel Nuchelmans]] to [[Lorenzo Valla]] in the 15th century, in later versions of his logic text traditionally called ''Dialectica''. Valla claimed that it was the appropriate Latin equivalent of the [[Greeks|Greek]] ''dilemmaton''. Nuchelmans argued that his probable source was a logic text of {{circa|1433}} of [[George of Trebizond]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nuchelmans |first1=Gabriel |title=Dilemmatic arguments : towards a history of their logic and rhetoric |date=1991 |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=0-444-85730-3 |page=89}}</ref> He also concluded that Valla had reintroduced to the Latin West a type of argument that had fallen into disuse.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nuchelmans |first1=Gabriel |title=Dilemmatic arguments : towards a history of their logic and rhetoric |date=1991 |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=0-444-85730-3 |page=94}}</ref>

Valla's [[neologism]] did not immediately take hold, preference being given to the established Latin term ''complexio'', used by [[Cicero]], with ''conversio'' applied to the upsetting of dilemmatic reasoning. With the support of [[Juan Luis Vives]], however, ''dilemma'' was widely applied by the end of the 16th century.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nuchelmans |first1=Gabriel |title=Dilemmatic arguments : towards a history of their logic and rhetoric |date=1991 |publisher=North-Holland |isbn=0-444-85730-3 |pages=102–6}}</ref>

A dilemma is often phrased as "you must accept either A, or B", where A and B are propositions, each leading to some subsequent conclusion. In the case where this is true, it can be called a "dichotomy", but when it is not true, the dilemma constitutes a [[false dichotomy]], which is a logical [[fallacy]]. Traditional usage distinguished the dilemma as a "horned [[syllogism]]" from the [[sophism]] that attracted the Latin name ''cornutus''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hamilton |first1=Sir William |title=The Logic of Sir William Hamilton, Bart |date=1863 |publisher=Moore, Wilstach & Baldwin |url=https://archive.org/details/logicsirwilliam00hamigoog |page=[https://archive.org/details/logicsirwilliam00hamigoog/page/n190 185] |language=en}}</ref> The original use of the word ''horns'' in English has been attributed to [[Nicholas Udall]] in his 1548 book ''Paraphrases'', translating from the Latin term ''cornuta interrogatio''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Erasmus |first1=Desiderius |title=Paraphrase on Luke 11-24 |date=2003 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |isbn=9780802036537 |url=https://archive.org/details/paraphraseonluke0048eras |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/paraphraseonluke0048eras/page/158 158] |language=en}}</ref>

==Dilemmatic arguments==
The dilemma is sometimes used as a [[rhetorical device]]. Its isolation as textbook material has been attributed to [[Hermogenes of Tarsus]] in his work ''On Invention''.<ref>Lucia Calboli Montefusco, ''Rhetorical use of dilemmatic arguments'', Rhetorica: A Journal of the History of Rhetoric Vol. 28, No. 4 (Autumn 2010), pp. 363–383, at p. 364. Published by: University of California Press on behalf of the International Society for the History of Rhetoric. DOI: 10.1525/rh.2010.28.4.363 {{JSTOR|10.1525/rh.2010.28.4.363}}</ref> [[C. S. Peirce]] gave a definition of ''dilemmatic argument'' as any argument relying on [[excluded middle]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ghosh |first1=Sujata |last2=Prasad |first2=Sanjiva |title=Logic and Its Applications: 7th Indian Conference, ICLA 2017, Kanpur, India, January 5-7, 2017, Proceedings |date=2016 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9783662540695 |page=177 note 5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=etrJDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA177 |language=en}}</ref>

===In logic===
In [[propositional logic]], ''dilemma'' is applied to a group of [[rules of inference]], which are in themselves valid rather than fallacious. They each have three premises, and include the [[constructive dilemma]] and [[destructive dilemma]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Church |first1=Alonzo |title=Introduction to Mathematical Logic |date=1996 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=0691029067 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JDLQOMKbdScC&pg=PA105 |language=en}}</ref> Such arguments can be refuted by showing that the disjunctive premise—the "horns of the dilemma"—does not, in fact, hold, because it presents a [[False dilemma|false dichotomy]]. One is asked to accept "A or B", but counters by showing that that is not all. Successfully undermining that premise is called "escaping through the horns of the dilemma".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Govier |first1=Trudy |title=A Practical Study of Argument |date=2009 |publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=978-0495603405 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IUxXbUvDiswC&pg=PA254 |language=en}}</ref>

===In philosophy===
Dilemmatic reasoning has been attributed to [[Melissus of Samos]], a [[Presocratic]] philosopher whose works survive in fragmentary form, making the origins of the technique in philosophy imponderable.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Harriman |first1=Benjamin |title=Melissus and Eleatic Monism |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781108416337 |page=44 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e091DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA44 |language=en}}</ref> It was established with [[Diodorus Cronus]] (died {{circa|284{{nbsp}}BCE|lk=no}}).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sedley |first1=David |title=Diodorus Cronus |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/diodorus-cronus |website=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |date=2018}}</ref> The paradoxes of [[Zeno of Elea]] were reported by [[Aristotle]] in dilemma form, but that may have been to conform with what [[Plato]] said about Zeno's style.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Palmer |first1=John |title=Zeno of Elea |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/zeno-elea/ |website=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |date=2017}}</ref>
[[File:Alarm dilemma.png|thumb|[[Contingency table]] of sounding (or not sounding) an alarm for a possible earthquake]]

===Moral dilemmas along with ethical dilemmas===
{{main|Ethical dilemma}}
In cases where two [[moral principle]]s appear to be inconsistent, an actor confronts a dilemma in terms of which principle to follow. This kind of moral case study is attributed to [[Cicero]], in book III of his ''[[De Officiis]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jonsen |first1=Albert R. |last2=Toulmin |first2=Stephen Edelston |title=The Abuse of Casuistry: A History of Moral Reasoning |date=1988 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520060630 |page=75 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RNipCKHdnlsC&pg=PA75 |language=en}}</ref> In the Christian tradition of [[casuistry]], an approach to abstract ranking of principles introduced by [[Bartolomé de Medina (theologian)|Bartolomé de Medina]] in the 16th century became tainted with the accusation of [[laxism]], as did casuistry itself.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Peters |first1=Francis E. |title=The words and will of God |date=2003 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=0691114617 |page=154 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=26aSVSICGIEC&pg=PA154 |language=en}}</ref> Another approach, with legal roots, is to lay emphasis on particular features present in a given case: in other words, the exact framing of the dilemma.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jonsen |first1=Albert R. |last2=Toulmin |first2=Stephen Edelston |title=The Abuse of Casuistry: A History of Moral Reasoning |date=1988 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520060630 |page=54 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RNipCKHdnlsC&pg=PA54 |language=en}}</ref>

=== In law ===
In law, [[Valentin Jeutner]] has argued that the term "legal dilemma" could be used as a [[wiktionary:term of art|term-of-art]], to describe a situation where a legal subject is confronted with two or more legal norms that the legal subject cannot simultaneously comply with.<ref>Birkenkötter, Hannah, ''Valentin Jeutner: Irresolvable Norm Conflicts in International Law: The Concept of a Legal Dilemma'', 28 (2017) European Journal of International Law 1415-1428.</ref>

Examples include contradictory contracts where one clause directly negates another clause, or conflicts between fundamental (e.g. [[Constitutional law|constitutional]]) legal norms. [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz's]] 1666 doctoral dissertation ''De casibus perplexis'' (Perplexing Cases) is an early study of contradictory legal conditions.<ref>Leibniz, Gottfried Wilhelm, "Inaugural Dissertation on Perplexing Cases in the Law" in Alberto Artosi, Bernardo Pieri, and Giovanni Sartor (eds.), ''Leibniz: Logico-Philosophical Puzzles in the Law'' (Springer 2013).</ref> In domestic law, it has been argued that the [[Federal Constitutional Court|German Constitutional Court]] confronted a legal dilemma when determining, in connection with proceedings relating to the German [[Luftsicherheitsgesetz|Aviation Security Act]], whether a government official could intentionally kill innocent civilians by shooting down a hijacked airplane that would otherwise have crashed into a football stadium, killing tens of thousands.<ref>Jeutner, Valentin (2017), [https://global.oup.com/academic/product/irresolvable-norm-conflicts-in-international-law-9780198808374?cc=se&lang=en& Irresolvable Norm Conflicts in International Law: The Concept of a Legal Dilemma], Oxford University Press, p. 15, 72. See also Michael Bohlander, ‘Of Shipwrecked Sailors, Unborn Children, Conjoined Twins and Hijacked Airplanes—Taking Human Life and the Defence of Necessity’ (2006) 70 The Journal of Criminal Law 147.</ref>

In international law, it has been suggested that the [[International Court of Justice]] confronted a legal dilemma in its 1996 [[International Court of Justice advisory opinion on the Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons|Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion]]. It was faced with the question whether, in an extreme circumstance of self-defence, it is a [[Self-defence in international law|state's right to self-defence]] or international law's general prohibition of [[nuclear weapon]]s that should take priority.<ref>Jeutner, Valentin (2017), [https://global.oup.com/academic/product/irresolvable-norm-conflicts-in-international-law-9780198808374?cc=se&lang=en& Irresolvable Norm Conflicts in International Law: The Concept of a Legal Dilemma], Oxford University Press, p. 10–11.</ref>
